structures.title: Basic SOV sentence order
structures.explanation: Korean puts the verb or adjective at the very end, with the subject and object before it. Particles mark each noun's role, so the order of subject and object can flex, but the predicate stays last. This is the core skeleton of every Korean sentence.
structures.ex2_ref: My younger sibling reads a book.

structures.title: Polite present tense
structures.explanation: Drop 다 from the dictionary form and add -아요 (if the last stem vowel is ㅏ/ㅗ) or -어요 (otherwise); 하다 becomes 해요. This is the everyday polite ending used to state present or habitual actions.

structures.title: Past tense
structures.explanation: Insert -았- (ㅏ/ㅗ stems) or -었- (other stems) before 어요; 하다 becomes 했어요. The past marker attaches to the stem and the sentence still ends politely.

structures.title: Future intention or plan
structures.explanation: Add -ㄹ 거예요 after a vowel stem and -을 거예요 after a consonant stem to express a plan or expectation about the future. It works for first-person intentions and general predictions.
structures.ex1_ref: I will watch a movie tomorrow.
structures.ex2_ref: I will rest at home this weekend.

structures.title: Identifying with 'to be'
structures.explanation: Attach 이에요 after a consonant-final noun and 예요 after a vowel-final noun to say 'is/am/are a ___'. The copula comes at the end just like a verb and matches the noun's final sound.

structures.title: Negating an action
structures.explanation: Put 안 right before the verb, or attach -지 않아요 to the stem; both negate the action equally. With 하다 verbs, 안 splits the noun and 하다 (공부 안 해요).

structures.title: Existence and possession
structures.explanation: 있어요 means 'there is / to have' and 없어요 means 'there isn't / to not have'. The noun in question takes the subject particle 이/가. The same pattern covers both location and ownership.
structures.ex2_ref: I don't have money right now.

structures.title: Polite honorific request
structures.explanation: Attach -세요 after a vowel stem or -으세요 after a consonant stem to make a respectful request or an honorific statement about someone senior. It raises the subject you are addressing.

structures.title: Comparing two things
structures.explanation: Mark the standard of comparison with 보다 ('than'); the adverb 더 ('more') is optional but common. The thing being compared takes 이/가 and the adjective ends the sentence.
structures.ex1_ref: Apples are more expensive than oranges.

structures.title: Expressing obligation
structures.explanation: Attach -아/어야 해요 (or 돼요) to a verb stem to say 'must' or 'have to'. It combines the connective -아/어야 with 하다/되다 and ends the sentence politely.
structures.ex2_ref: I have to take medicine every day.

structures.title: Relative clause modifying a noun
structures.explanation: A modifying clause comes before the noun it describes, with the verb taking -는 for a present action. Korean has no 'who/which' word; the whole clause simply precedes the noun.
structures.ex1_ref: Who is the person who lives here?
structures.ex2_ref: The food I like is kimchi stew.

structures.title: Wanting to do something
structures.explanation: Attach -고 싶어요 to a verb stem to express the speaker's wish to do that action. For a third person's desire, use -고 싶어 해요 instead.
structures.ex2_ref: I want to go to the sea.

structures.title: Present progressive
structures.explanation: Attach -고 있어요 to a verb stem to say an action is in progress right now, like the English '-ing'. Use 계시다 (계세요) for an honorific subject.
structures.ex2_ref: I am waiting for a friend.

structures.title: Superlative (the most)
structures.explanation: Put 가장 or 제일 ('most') before the adjective to form the superlative; the two words are interchangeable and 제일 is more conversational. It ranks one item highest among a group.
structures.ex1_ref: Baekdu Mountain is the highest in Korea.
structures.ex2_ref: This restaurant is the most delicious.

structures.title: Expressing ability
structures.explanation: Attach -ㄹ 수 있어요 after a vowel stem or -을 수 있어요 after a consonant stem to say 'can'. Replace 있어요 with 없어요 to say 'cannot'.

structures.title: Conditional 'if / when'
structures.explanation: Attach -면 after a vowel stem or -으면 after a consonant stem to introduce a condition; the result clause follows. It covers both real 'when' situations and hypothetical 'if' ones.
structures.ex1_ref: If I have time, I will go.
